extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students (litigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards governing who can be held liable for patent infringement (public bodies, private corporations, officers, co-owners, assignors, licensees, and assignees), and the scope/limits of licenses and assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of municipal corporations and city instrumentalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where seats embodying this invention were bought by the Board of Education of the city of New York for the use of the schools ... the city is clearly to be a proper party to account for these savings or profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An instrumentality or corporate department through which a city's educational interests are carried may expose the city itself to suit to account for profits from infringement. The proper party to proceed against is the one that has received the profits; if the city has saved or made anything by the infringement, it is a proper party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public bodies non-corporate: limited liability; contractors/officers answerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Public bodies which are not corporations ... are not capable of committing an infringement or any other wrong except those specified in the statute which creates them; contractors and officials acting for such bodies are alone answerable for their unauthorized appropriation of a patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a public body is merely a collection of individuals exercising statutory powers (and not a corporation), the statute creating them determines liability; ordinarily contractors and officials who actually commit the infringing acts are personally liable rather than the public body itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor-supplied infringing articles: hirer's liability depends on circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A public body, employing a contractor to furnish articles for its buildings, is not liable for infringements by the contractor in supplying patented articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: a public body using the product made by an infringing contractor is not automatically liable. Exceptions exist (e.g., where municipality is liable by reason of being a municipal corporation or other specific circumstances). Cases: May v. Juneau Co.; Brown v. District of Columbia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private corporation liable for acts of agents/employees authorized or ratified by it
rubrics_metrics.description: A private corporation infringes by any act of its agents or employees, authorized or ratified by it, which wrongfully appropriates the patented invention. By procuring infringing devices and permitting its workmen to use them, by hiring contractors to practise the invention for its benefit, ... it may commit a direct act of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations cannot escape liability by disguising transactions; accepting benefits of infringing acts renders the corporation liable. Examples: procuring infringing devices, permitting employees to use them, hiring contractors to practice the invention for corporate benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation cannot avoid liability by corporate structure/disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not permitted to escape responsibility by any disguise of its transactions, and to accept, however indirectly, the benefit of the infringing acts of its officers and servants, renders it liable to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where stockholders organize a separate corporation in another state and carry on business with their own employees and machinery, the corporation whose affairs are thus conducted is still the actual infringer and answerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability of officers, directors, and stockholders: three competing views
rubrics_metrics.description: One opinion regards the infringing act as the act of the corporation alone; another considers directors, agents, and other servants actually employing or authorizing the employment of the patented invention as guilty and personally answerable; a third treats stockholders as infringers by reason of acceptance of benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise favors the second view as harmonizing with patent law: agents who perform infringing acts and corporate officers who authorize them may be personally responsible. Workmen and innocent employees generally are not infringers. Stockholders ordinarily are not liable unless they take active part or accept the benefit in a way that makes them participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoinment of corporate officers/participants
rubrics_metrics.description: They may be enjoined whenever this is necessary to protect the patentee against future infringements; officers of an infringing corporation may be enjoined even if not liable for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief (injunction) can name officers, directors, and others as defendants and enjoin them individually to prevent further infringement; damages claims against individuals are more restricted and vary by jurisdiction and doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of the principal who hires a contractor to use an infringing device
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the contractor is hired and to work for the corporation and to use the infringing device, the hirer is probably liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the principal hires a contractor with knowledge (or the contractor is acting under a license but does not pay royalties), different outcomes follow (see Stow v. Chicago; Jacobs v. Board of Commissioners). The principal may not escape liability by claiming ignorance if the contractor was hired to perform infringing acts for the principal's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability where corporate officers act affirmatively to order infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A director who has acted affirmatively ... and ordered an infringement by the corporation, would subject himself to an action. Infringement is not a trespass but a case; if the officer acted in the business or employment of the corporation and the corporation adopted and approved the act, the officer will be deemed to have authorized it and be bound by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers who order or authorize infringement (e.g., instruct agent to manufacture infringing articles and then market them) risk personal liability. Mere passive position or lack of direct participation reduces likelihood of personal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of joint-owners of a patent against co-owners
rubrics_metrics.description: One of two or more co-owners of a patented invention may be guilty of infringement as against the others ... his departure from the patented invention, as described and claimed in the patent, puts him in the same position as a non-owner, and renders him liable in the same manner to the other owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-owners are generally free to use the patent as owners, but using other arts or articles that embody the substance of the patent while adding features that give advantage over co-owners is prohibited; damages are apportioned to other owners according to their shares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignments: assignor vs assignee rights and liabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment either transfers the entire interest of the assignor in a patented invention, or makes him a co-owner with the assignee. In the former case, the assignor becomes a stranger to the patent and capable of infringement by any act of unauthorized manufacture, use, or sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assignment conveys entire interest, assignor may later infringe as a stranger. If assignment creates co-ownership, the assignor has same rights and liabilities as a co-owner. Grantor is a stranger outside the territory exclusively conveyed to grantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial limits of conveyances and resulting infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A grantor is a stranger to the patent within the territory exclusively conveyed to his grantee, while the grantee is a stranger outside the limits of such territory; each may thus invade the other's rights by usual methods of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments can be territorial; acts outside assigned territory can constitute infringement against the other party. Parties should observe territorial scope of assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of a license: express vs implied; estoppel effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A license transfers an interest in the invention and estops the licensor from interfering with the enjoyment of such interest by asserting his monopoly against the licensee. If the license is an express license, the rights of the licensee and the estoppel against the licensor are defined by its specific terms. If the license is implied, the duties and obligations of the parties are defined by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No license can convey an interest or work an estoppel unless the licensor was an owner of the patent at the time the license was granted. Determine scope by the instrument's terms (express) or by surrounding circumstances (implied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee within scope: non-infringement while acting under license
rubrics_metrics.description: While acting under his license, and within the scope of the interest it confers, the licensee does not infringe the patent, and on a failure to perform his own part of the agreement is liable only to an action on the contract in the local courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee operating within the express or implied scope is protected from infringement suits by the licensor; contractual remedies apply for breach of payment/royalty obligations unless the license contains a forfeiture clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions, forfeiture, and rescission of licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: If the license is granted on conditions, it affords no protection to the licensee unless the conditions are fulfilled, though late authorities declare that it must be rescinded by agreement, or by a decree in equity, before an action for infringement can be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a condition precedent fails, the licensor must typically rescind the license (by agreement or equity) before bringing an infringement action; a mere claim of forfeiture in the license may not automatically re-create infringement without proper notice or procedure depending on jurisdiction and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts beyond the license (territory, period, manner) constitute infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee infringes by the practice of any other patented invention than the one covered by his license, or by employing that in any other manner than his license specifies ... Where a license permits use only in one place, it is an infringement to use elsewhere; use beyond territorial limits or period is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using licensed invention outside licensed place; making or selling outside the grantee's territory; using during extension periods without exercising options and paying fees; using more machines than licensed. Courts treat acts outside defined scope as infringing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee repudiation/abandonment or defense on other grounds forfeits protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee repudiating the license, or abandoning it, or claiming his right against the licensor on other grounds, forfeits the privilege which it confers and can no longer set up its estoppel against the licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a licensee repudiates or treats the license as void, he may be treated as a stranger and subject to infringement suits. Cases: Bell v. McCullough; Hat Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Porter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee's failure to pay royalties: not automatically an infringer absent forfeiture clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee merely refusing to pay his royalties cannot be treated as an infringer; a licensor cannot sue his licensee for infringement upon a failure to pay royalties unless the license contains a clause of forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent an express forfeiture clause, the licensor's remedy for unpaid royalties is typically contract actions, not infringement suits. Some licenses provide forfeiture upon nonpayment; follow terms of agreement and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee making different article or practicing other patents: not protected by original license
rubrics_metrics.description: The license to make an article described in the patent does not protect the licensee if he makes one different from the one described; a license under one patent affords no protection against another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees cannot shelter acts that make/use/sell different inventions (even if related) or other claims/patents. If licensee makes the licensor's invention under a different name or practices an additional patented invention not covered, liability for infringement may arise and agreed fees remain payable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee selling materials to known non-licensees may be liable
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee authorized to sell materials to be used in a patented process infringes by selling to others who are known not to be licensees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplying components or materials to unlicensed third parties who then practice the patented invention can trigger liability; courts have found infringement where licensee knowingly supplies non-licensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability of license: assignee inherits same limitations and may infringe likewise
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a license is assignable, the assignee rests under the same limitations as the original licensee, and may infringe the patent by the same modes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignees do not gain broader rights than the original license; they take subject to territorial, temporal, and other limitations. Some cases discuss whether assignment changes liability for acts performed by the assignee.
